strengths: Important methodological contribution: The paper addresses a major conceptual flaw in audio chaptering literature, namely the transcript-dependence and sentence-discretization bias of traditional text-segmentation metrics. Formalizing transcript-invariant time-space protocols (T1 and T2) provides a standardized evaluation foundation for future work.

Comprehensive empirical investigation: The authors systematically evaluate three distinct modeling paradigms (text-based with acoustic feature fusion, end-to-end audio-only AudioSeg, and multimodal LLMs) across various dimensions including transcript quality, audio duration, and speaker regimes.

Strong and insightful findings: The paper presents compelling evidence that AudioSeg (particularly using Whisper representations) substantially outperforms text-only pipelines, and provides actionable insights (e.g., pause duration and non-speech audio cues like transitional music drive most acoustic gains; speaker diarization features specifically benefit multi-speaker content).

High clarity and reproducibility: The paper is clearly structured, with detailed descriptions of feature extraction, alignment procedures, prompt engineering, and training hyperparameters in the appendix.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to a single dataset (YTSeg): While YTSeg is large and diverse, it comprises English YouTube videos whose chapter conventions and editing styles (e.g., sound cues, visual-driven pauses) may differ significantly from other domains like conversational podcasts, radio broadcasts, or academic lectures.

Asymmetry in model capabilities: MLLMs are evaluated in a setup where they simultaneously generate transcripts, boundaries, and chapter titles, whereas AudioSeg and MiniSeg focus strictly on boundary detection. The qualitative aspect of chaptering (e.g., title generation and semantic coherence of identified sections) is not evaluated.

Confounding nature of the Whisper encoder: The best-performing audio-only model relies on Whisper-Large as an audio feature extractor. Because Whisper is trained on speech transcription, it encodes extensive linguistic and semantic knowledge rather than purely acoustic features, making the distinction between 'audio-only' and 'speech-derived linguistic features' somewhat blurred.

strengths: The paper addresses a critical and historically overlooked gap in the literature: chaptering has long been treated as a downstream text-segmentation task, inheriting text-based evaluation protocols that suffer from severe discretization loss and transcript dependence.

The conceptual formalization of evaluation protocols (R1, H1-H3 vs. time-space T1 and T2) is rigorous and clearly articulated. The oracle discretization ceiling experiment (Table A5) convincingly proves why time-invariant metrics are necessary.

The experimental scope is remarkably comprehensive, systematically comparing text-based baselines, hand-crafted acoustic features, an audio-only architecture (AudioSeg) with diverse encoders, and multimodal LLMs under multiple inference paradigms (zero-shot, ICL, cascaded, LoRA).

The empirical findings are actionable and insightful, revealing that non-speech cues (music, transition sound effects) strongly aid AudioSeg, pause duration drives the vast majority of acoustic gains in text-based models, and ASR word error rate does not straightforwardly dictate segmentation quality.
The paper is very well written and structured, with thorough appendices covering implementation details, feature extraction formulas, diarization protocols, and error analyses.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to a single dataset (YTSeg), which primarily features English YouTube videos. Because YouTube videos often have distinct production conventions (e.g., musical stings and transition jingles), some findings—particularly the strong benefit of non-speech acoustic cues—may not generalize equally to other long-form domains like unedited lectures or podcasts.

Although continuous-time evaluation (Protocol T2) is introduced and advocated in Section 2.3.2 as the most natural formulation of the task, all main tables and figures report discretized chunks under Protocol T1. Reporting collar-based T2 metrics across varying tolerance windows (e.g., ±5s, ±15s, ±30s) would have strengthened the validation of the continuous-time proposal.

The paper focuses exclusively on boundary identification and excludes chapter title generation. While this boundary-focused scope is methodologically sound for benchmarking segmentation, full chaptering in practical deployments (and in the MLLM prompts tested) entails titling as well.

strengths: The paper provides a much-needed formalization of evaluation protocols for audio chaptering, clearly elucidating the flaws and discretization loss (oracle ceiling around 73-81%) of sentence-snapped text-space metrics (R1-H3) and proposing transcript-invariant time-space metrics (T1, T2).

Comprehensive empirical benchmarking across three distinct paradigms: text-based architectures augmented with prosodic/acoustic features, an audio-only architecture (AudioSeg), and multimodal LLMs (Qwen-Omni series).

Valuable analytical insights, including the ablation demonstrating that pause duration and non-speech audio cues (e.g., music/transitions ablated via DeepFilterNet) contribute substantially to boundary detection, as well as the fine-grained analysis on speaker regimes showing that speaker diarization features specifically help multi-speaker recordings.
Well-written, clearly organized, and thoroughly documented with extensive appendices covering alignment details, exact prompts, hyperparameter configurations, and failure mode analyses.
weaknesses: Experiments are restricted to a single dataset (YTSeg), which consists exclusively of English YouTube videos; evaluating across different genres (such as meetings, long academic lectures, or dedicated podcast corpora like the Spotify podcast dataset) would better validate the generalizability of the findings.

The strong performance of the 'audio-only' AudioSeg relies heavily on the Whisper encoder (F1 45.52 vs. HuBERT Base 31.07 and HuBERT Large 35.58), which was pre-trained on hundreds of thousands of hours of speech recognition data and inherently encapsulates linguistic knowledge. Without Whisper, purely self-supervised acoustic encoders underperform text-based models, a distinction that deserves more prominent discussion.

Although continuous-time evaluation (Protocol T2) is proposed and motivated as the cleanest formalization of the task, the main empirical tables exclusively report discrete time (T1 @ 6s); reporting collar-based F1 across varying tolerance windows under T2 would have substantially strengthened the evaluation section.

Comparisons involving multimodal LLMs are constrained to audio under 30 minutes due to context length limitations, and chunk-based streaming approaches suffered heavily from generation loops, leaving the full-length video regime unaddressed for MLLMs.

strengths: The paper addresses a critical and long-standing methodological flaw in audio chaptering and spoken text segmentation: the reliance on transcript-dependent discretization and evaluation. The formalization and empirical comparison of text-space (R1, H1–H3) and time-space (T1, T2) protocols provide much-needed clarity and a reproducible framework for future research.

The empirical investigation is comprehensive and carefully executed across three distinct paradigms (text-based with acoustic augmentation, audio-only, and multimodal LLMs), supported by insightful analyses across video duration, speaker composition, and acoustic feature types.

The proposed AudioSeg model achieves impressive results, demonstrating that learned representations from speech encoders (specifically Whisper Large) can substantially outperform traditional text-based pipelines.

The analysis of multimodal LLMs (Qwen-Omni series) provides valuable diagnostic insights, clearly isolating the bottleneck in direct temporal grounding versus segmentation capacity, as evidenced by the dramatic jump in performance when coupling text outputs with forced alignment.

The ablation study isolating non-speech cues via DeepFilterNet is an elegant demonstration of how audio captures transition signals (e.g., jingles, sound effects) that are entirely invisible to pure text transcripts.
weaknesses: The conceptual distinction between 'audio-only' and 'text-based' is somewhat blurred by the choice of encoder in AudioSeg. As shown in Table 6, AudioSeg's high performance is heavily dependent on the Whisper Large encoder (F1=45.52), whereas pure audio/acoustic pre-trained encoders (HuBERT, PEA-Frame, Qwen3-AuT) achieve much lower scores (F1=24.66–35.58). Because Whisper is explicitly trained on massive amounts of transcribed speech, its internal representations encode substantial implicit linguistic knowledge, which warrants deeper discussion.

The empirical findings are predominantly drawn from YTSeg (YouTube videos), where creators frequently introduce explicit acoustic styling (intro music, sound effects, clear rhetorical pauses) at chapter transitions. Although AMI is evaluated as an out-of-domain benchmark, the sample size is small (4 test meetings in the <30 min bucket and 16 overall), leaving open questions about generalizability to conversational speech lacking produced transition cues.
Due to context length constraints, MLLM evaluations are restricted to audio under 30 minutes, meaning the longest, most challenging real-world chaptering scenarios are unexplored for this paradigm.

strengths: Important and well-motivated problem: The paper critically re-examines the conventional transcript-centric framing of audio chaptering, clearly articulating why sentence-snapped, text-space evaluation is inherently lossy and confounded by ASR granularity.

Methodological clarity and formalization: The formalization of transcript-invariant time-space evaluation protocols (discrete T1 and continuous collar-based T2) provides a rigorous, standardized foundation for comparing text, audio, and multimodal systems.

Strong and systematic empirical study: The paper conducts an extensive set of experiments covering three modeling paradigms (text-based, audio-only AudioSeg, and MLLMs), investigating ASR degradation, individual acoustic feature contributions, duration effects, speaker counts, and out-of-domain transfer on AMI.

Valuable empirical findings: The work presents insightful takeaways, such as the fact that Whisper-encoded audio-only representations outperform text-based models, pauses drive the majority of acoustic gains, and MLLMs struggle significantly with continuous temporal grounding despite identifying high-level topics.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on ASR-pretrained audio representations: AudioSeg's superior performance relies heavily on the Whisper Large encoder (45.52 F1) compared to purely self-supervised or acoustic encoders like HuBERT (35.58 F1) or PEA-Frame (31.36 F1). While the authors acknowledge that Whisper implicitly captures linguistic content, more discussion could be dedicated to disentangling how much of AudioSeg's gain is due to acoustic boundary cues (e.g., transition jingles) versus implicit lexical understanding encoded in Whisper.

Domain and data diversity: Experiments rely primarily on the YTSeg corpus, which reflects specific YouTube editing conventions (e.g., music transitions, intentional chapter structuring). While the authors include AMI evaluation to show transfer, AMI is relatively small and differs significantly in task definition.

Scale limitations in MLLM experiments: Due to computational constraints, larger models like Qwen3-Omni were evaluated only via zero-shot/ICL and restricted to recordings under 30 minutes, leaving questions about how fine-tuned long-context multimodal foundation models would perform against dedicated architectures like AudioSeg.

strengths: Addresses a fundamental methodological flaw in the audio chaptering literature: the reliance on transcript-dependent text-space segmentation metrics that bias evaluations and conflate ASR sentence granularity with actual boundary accuracy.

Formulates and rigorously validates transcript-invariant time-space evaluation protocols (both discrete T1 and continuous collar-based T2), demonstrating their robustness and establishing clear standards for cross-paradigm comparisons.

Presents a clean and effective audio-only architecture (AudioSeg) using learned speech representations; results convincingly demonstrate that audio encoders (especially Whisper Large) capture essential structural and non-speech cues (e.g., transition music, jingles, pauses) that text-based pipelines miss.

Conducts thorough and well-designed empirical analyses across multiple dimensions, including acoustic feature ablations (showing pauses and speaker cues dominate), ASR error robustness, duration regimes, speaker composition, and out-of-domain generalization to the AMI corpus.

Provides illuminating insights into multimodal LLM behavior on long-form audio, demonstrating that while MLLMs possess topical segmentation capability, their direct temporal grounding remains poor without forced alignment.
weaknesses: The empirical validation is confined entirely to English datasets (YTSeg and AMI), leaving open questions regarding cross-lingual transfer and applicability to lower-resource or non-English speech.

AudioSeg is trained and evaluated using a fixed 6-second window discretization; while Table A8 explores other chunk sizes, re-binning artifacts arise because the underlying model operates at a fixed grid rather than native continuous-time boundary detection.

Due to computational constraints, the exploration of foundation MLLMs is somewhat limited in training scale (e.g., fine-tuning was only performed on Qwen2.5-Omni 7B, omitting the stronger Qwen3-Omni).

While the paper compares text models augmented with hand-crafted acoustic features against learned audio-only models, it does not evaluate a hybrid architecture combining learned text embeddings (e.g., MiniLM/RoBERTa) directly with learned frame-level audio representations (e.g., Whisper encoder) in an explicit multimodal fusion setup.
